problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}\,m$ and the particle has velocity $v=8\,m/s$ when its displacement is $\pi \,m,$ find the value of $k.$
worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/b396b80995e34fe348b3d059737b1eec3d4ce5a9d2e9138a8e7d4ed5c0945dc0.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=\frac{\pi }{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =-k\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Finally, since $v=8\,m/s$ when $x=\pi \,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\ 32 & =8+k \\ k & =24.\end{aligned}
$$
